1. Market Overview & Long-Term Price Trend

Gold has appreciated from $273.90 in August 2000 to $5,377.30 as of March 2026 — a 19.6× nominal increase. The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over this ~25.5-year span is 12.38%, outperforming most major equity indices on a risk-adjusted basis (Sharpe-like ratio of 0.70).

2. Volatility Analysis & Regime Detection

Volatility regime detection is the highest-value analytical dimension for gold. Using a 90-day rolling standard deviation of daily log returns (annualized), we classify each trading day into one of four regimes based on percentile thresholds:

  • Low Volatility — below median (~15.5% ann.)
  • Medium Volatility — median to 75th percentile (~15.5–18.4% ann.)
  • High Volatility — 75th to 90th percentile (~18.4–23.7% ann.)
  • Crisis — above 90th percentile (>23.7% ann.)
Figure 2. 30-day and 90-day rolling annualized volatility with regime threshold bands. Crisis episodes shaded in red.

This reflects gold's convexity: volatility spikes often coincide with risk-off episodes where gold appreciates as a safe-haven asset. However, realized volatility during these periods is nearly double the low-vol baseline, demanding active position sizing.

3. Seasonal & Calendar-Based Patterns

We test for statistically significant seasonal effects using one-way ANOVA across months and days of week, supplemented by one-sample t-tests against zero.

Monthly Returns

ANOVA result: F = 0.83, p = 0.613 — we fail to reject the null hypothesis of equal monthly means. Observed differences are likely noise.

That said, January (+2.32% avg, p = 0.014) and August (+1.97% avg, p = 0.031) show marginal statistical significance. June is the weakest month (–0.92% avg), though not significant (p = 0.347).

Day-of-Week Returns

ANOVA result: F = 0.79, p = 0.534 — no significant difference across weekdays.

Friday (+0.093% avg, p = 0.005) and Monday (+0.065% avg, p = 0.041) are marginally significant, possibly reflecting weekend risk-premium accumulation and rebalancing flows.

Figure 4. Average monthly and day-of-week returns with ±1 standard-error bars. Green = positive; red = negative.
Figure 5. Monthly return heatmap by year. Visual inspection confirms high cross-sectional variance — no consistently dominant month.
Bottom line for allocation: Seasonal edges in gold are weak and statistically unreliable. Any tactical allocation based on calendar effects should be sized conservatively and treated as a low-conviction overlay rather than a core signal.

4. Return Distribution & Tail Risk

Gold's daily return distribution deviates markedly from normality. The Jarque-Bera test strongly rejects normality (JB = 11,459, p < 0.001).

Figure 6. Left: Histogram of daily returns with normal overlay and VaR thresholds. Right: Q-Q plot showing fat tails and mild left skew.

The negative skew (–0.32) and high excess kurtosis (+6.53) indicate:

  • Fat tails — extreme moves occur far more often than a normal distribution predicts.
  • Mild left skew — large negative surprises are slightly more frequent than large positive ones, though the largest single-day move was actually a loss (–11.37% on 2026-01-30).
  • Convex crisis behavior — during stress, gold often rallies (positive tail), but liquidity crunches can generate sharp temporary selloffs.
Risk management implication: A 99% VaR of –3.05% implies that on 1% of trading days, gold loses more than 3% in a single session. For a $100M allocation, that is a >$3M daily mark-to-market swing. Position sizing and options overlays should account for this tail thickness, not a Gaussian assumption.

5. Momentum Dynamics & Liquidity Behavior

Moving Average Crossover Signals

We evaluate a simple 50-day / 200-day moving-average crossover as a proxy for trend-following momentum. Gold has been in a "bull regime" (MA50 > MA200) for 70.8% of the dataset — consistent with its secular uptrend.

Figure 7. Gold price with 50-day and 200-day moving averages. Green shading indicates bull regime (MA50 > MA200).
Signal Regime% of TimeFwd 5-DayFwd 20-DayFwd 60-Day
Bull (MA50 > MA200)70.8%+0.28%+1.17%+3.41%
Bear (MA50 < MA200)29.2%+0.21%+0.68%+2.10%

Even in bear-regime periods, forward returns remain positive — gold's long-term drift dominates short-term momentum signals. The crossover adds marginal value in timing entry points but is not a reliable short signal.

Volume & Liquidity Profile

Volume data in the early years (2000–2003) is sparse and unreliable (frequent zero-volume days). Post-2004, volume stabilizes with a weak negative correlation to absolute returns (r = –0.025), suggesting that higher volume does not systematically coincide with larger price moves in gold — unlike equity markets where volume typically confirms volatility.

Figure 8. Left: Trading volume over time (post-2004) with 60-day moving average. Right: Scatter of absolute daily return vs volume.
Liquidity note: Average daily volume is 4,283 contracts. Volume spikes (>2σ above 20-day average) occurred on 210 days post-2004. On these days, average absolute return was 0.74% — only modestly above the unconditional 0.70% mean. Gold's liquidity profile appears relatively stable even during stress, though the current 2026 regime warrants monitoring given parabolic price action.

Scenario Framework

  • Bull case ($6,000+ target): Continued central-bank buying, escalation of geopolitical fragmentation, and sustained negative real rates in DM economies. Probability: moderate.
  • Base case ($4,500–$5,500 range): Volatility mean-reverts to 18–22%; price consolidates as rate-cut expectations stabilize. Probability: highest.
  • Bear case ($3,500–$4,000): Sharp risk-on rotation, USD strength, or coordinated CB intervention triggers a –20% to –30% correction similar to 2013 or 2022. Probability: moderate — elevated given current vol.
Final recommendation: Maintain strategic allocation but implement volatility targeting (reduce notional when 90-day vol > 25%). Consider put spreads or collar structures to monetize elevated implied vol. Do not chase momentum at current levels without a defined stop-loss framework.
